title: I Heart Huckabees
full_review:
If nothing else, "I Heart Huckabees" (Fox Searchlight) is a clever movie. In fact, for most of its 105 minutes, director David O. Russell proceeds to show viewers just how clever a film it is, or more specifically, how clever a filmmaker he is. What he fails to recognize, however, is the dangerously thin distinction between ingenious and ingenuous.
What's it all about? Well, that's precisely the philosophical conundrum at the "Heart" of "Huckabees." Billed as an existential comedy, "I Heart Huckabees" is a film that is hard to label and even harder to explain. It is a madcap mix of highbrow humor and lowbrow slapstick, a screwball comedy for eggheads full of metaphysical musings about the meaning of life, with dollops of quantum physics tossed in for good measure; all of which adds up to little more than window dressing on a strange, but rather, thin story.

Jason Schwartzman plays Albert Markovski, an angst-ridden environmental activist perplexed by a series of coincidences involving a Sudanese doorman. In an effort to connect the dots, he hires Bernard and Vivian Jaffe (Dustin Hoffman and Lily Tomlin), a married team of existential detectives, who unravel mysteries at the core of their clients' innermost being.

In short order, the oddball sleuths -- a tribute to the Powell-Loy pairing in "The Thin Man" series -- begin to spy on Albert's daily activities, including a funny scene where Vivian takes notes while perched on the ledge outside his kitchen window. Their investigation zeros in on Albert's festering animosity toward Brad Stand (Jude Law), an uber-ambitious executive climbing the corporate ladder at a Wal-Mart-like retail chain called Huckabees.

Things get really confusing when, in a table-turning tit-for-tat, Brad also employs Bernard's and Vivian's services, a move which has unforeseen fashion effects on his girlfriend Dawn (a bikini-clad Naomi Watts), Huckabees' golden-girl spokesmodel.
When Albert proves a tough case to crack, he is paired up with hot-headed Tommy (Mark Wahlberg), a petroleum-preoccupied firefighter and uncompromising truth seeker. Tommy lures Albert away from Bernard and Vivian and into the camp of their sexy archrival -- and one-time prize student -- Caterine Vauban (Isabelle Huppert). Unlike Bernard and Vivian, Vauban, a French nihilist, subscribes to a Sartrean view that life has no purpose; she even has business cards which read: "Cruelty, Manipulation and Meaninglessness."

Russell, whose resume includes such offbeat efforts as "Flirting with Disaster" (1996) and "Three Kings" (1999), continues to be one of the most original voices in Hollywood, a town with a pronounced tendency toward the conventional and the derivative. In an age of crash-and-smash cinema, Russell deserves credit for making a picture which targets the intellect instead of the adrenal glands. However, what eludes him is the fact that for a movie to really work, it must appeal, not only to the head, but to the heart, which, in spite of its title, is exactly what his emotionally hollow film is sorely missing.

The ensemble cast is top-notch across the board, and includes some interesting cameos, among them Talia Shire (Schwartzman's real-life mom) as Albert's mother and Tippi Hedren (of Hitchcock's "The Birds" fame) as one of Albert's fellow tree-huggers.

While the eccentric concept is intriguing, the overall writing lacks the sharpness and wit of Charlie Kaufman, whose screenplays for films like "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" mine similar absurdist terrain without relegating story and character to the back seat. The same goes for Woody Allen, whose comedies have an analogous intellectually elitist bent, but don't require advanced degrees in philosophy in order to enjoy them.

Due to a sexual encounter and much rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
